screens.title: Introduction to Bash Scripting for Automation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Bash scripting matters for system administration and how to get started safely. Bash is more than an interactive shell: it is a scripting language that lets you sequence commands, use variables, make decisions, loop over items, and redirect input and output. That combination is what makes repetitive maintenance, log processing, and simple orchestration reliable and repeatable. You will see how the shebang selects the interpreter, why making a script executable matters, and how comments and small tests make scripts maintainable. We will work through variable usage, including positional parameters and special variables such as the exit status, and explore conditionals, loops, and redirection patterns you will use every day. Along the way you will practice a hands-on script that analyzes a directory for counts and disk usage, and you will learn common pitfalls like failing to quote variables or mixing string and numeric operators. By the end, you will be able to write, run, and troubleshoot small Bash scripts that save time and reduce mistakes. Think about one repetitive task you do now — scripting it is the next step.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Introduction
Introduction to Bash Scripting for Automation
Automate routine system tasks with scripts that run reliably. Learn execution, variables, flow control, and redirection that power daily administration.
Scripting Concept Map
Shebang → Variables → Flow → I/O → Automation
Shebang
Variables
Control Flow
Explore Key Topics
Shebang & Execution
Choose the interpreter and make scripts executable so behavior is predictable across systems.
Variables & Special Vars
Use named and positional variables plus exit status to pass data and check success or failure.
Flow & I/O
If, loops, echo, read, and redirection allow scripts to react, iterate, and handle files safely.
In this lesson we build practical habits: comment clearly, quote variables, check exit codes, and test scripts incrementally.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately. First, you will explain why Bash scripting is central to Linux administration: it lets you automate repetitive tasks, reduce human error, and capture knowledge in reusable scripts. As an example, think of a daily log rotation check that you can turn into a script and run automatically. Second, you will write basic Bash scripts: you will include a shebang so the OS invokes the intended interpreter, add comments for maintainability, set executable permissions, and run scripts from the shell. Practice creating a simple script that prints a startup message, then make it executable and run it. Third, you will declare and use variables: assign values, reference them with the dollar sign, and use braces to avoid ambiguity when concatenating strings. Fourth, you will understand key special variables such as positional parameters, the argument count, and the last command exit status. Each skill is framed with why it matters and a small mnemonic so you can recall correct practice under pressure.

screens.title: What is Bash and why automate with it?
screens.narratorSegment: Bash, short for the Bourne Again SHell, is both an interactive command interpreter and a scripting language used across Linux systems. As an interpreter it runs commands you type; as a scripting language it executes statements saved in a file, so you can repeat tasks reliably. Automation is the reason we script: repetitive operations like backups, log rotation checks, or user provisioning are error-prone when done manually. A script captures the correct sequence and lets you run it unattended. For example, a short script that archives logs and rotates permissions will run the same way every time, eliminating small mistakes. A common misconception is that Bash is only for ad-hoc commands; in reality, small to medium automation tasks are an ideal fit. Another misconception is confusion between systemd timers and Bash scripts — they complement each other: timers schedule, scripts perform the work. When beginning, favor clear, well-commented scripts that test exit codes and report failures. Finally, remember portability: using the shebang and POSIX-compatible constructs helps scripts behave consistently across distributions. How might scripting one routine task today free time for higher-value work?

keyIdea.title: Bash is automation glue
keyIdea.text: Bash ties commands together with logic and I/O so administrators can codify procedures and reduce manual errors.

content.html:
Definition
Bash: Interpreter and Scripting Language

Bash executes typed commands and runs scripts saved in files. Scripts combine commands with variables, flow control, and I/O so tasks become repeatable and testable.

  • Why automate: reduces errors, saves time, documents procedures.
  • Best uses: small system tasks—backups, checks, maintenance scripts.
  • Misconception: Bash can and should be used for small automation; larger orchestration may use other tools but Bash remains key for local tasks.
Example
A simple archival command sequence turned into a script ensures the same tar and chown commands run reliably across hosts.
Key Takeaway

Treat Bash scripts as documented, repeatable recipes. Start small, test, and capture common tasks.

Analogy
Think of a script as a checklist that runs itself. Instead of remembering steps, you run the script and it performs each verified step in order.
Command snapshot
#!/bin/bash

# Archive logs and set permissions
TARGET=/var/log/myapp
tar -czf /tmp/myapp-logs.tar.gz "$TARGET"
chown root:root /tmp/myapp-logs.tar.gz
Try: save, make executable with chmod +x, and run. Check exit codes after critical commands to detect failures.

screens.title: Script execution: shebang, permission, and running
screens.narratorSegment: Script execution starts with the shebang line. The shebang is a special first line beginning with a hash and exclamation mark followed by the interpreter path, typically /bin/bash. It tells the kernel which program should interpret the script when you run it directly. Without the shebang, the system may default to another shell or require you to invoke the interpreter explicitly. After saving a script, you must set the executable bit using chmod +x so the kernel permits execution. Running a script from the current directory requires an explicit path like dot-slash script name to avoid running a same-named command from the PATH. A common workflow: create the file, add a concise shebang and comments, chmod it executable, and then run small tests. Check the exit status variable after critical operations to detect failures. A frequent mistake is forgetting chmod or assuming the shell will auto-detect the interpreter. Another issue is using a non-portable shebang path; when portability matters, use env in the shebang to locate bash. Practice: create a tiny script that prints a message, chmod it, and run it with different users to observe permission behavior. What step would you add to validate the script before production?

keyIdea.title: Shebang and execute bits
keyIdea.text: Use a clear shebang and chmod +x to make script behavior predictable and executable by the intended interpreter.

content.html:
Execution Steps
1. Add shebang: #!/bin/bash
2. Add comments and logic
3. Make executable: chmod +x myscript.sh
4. Run with explicit path: ./myscript.sh
Tip: Use #!/usr/bin/env bash when you need portability across systems with different bash locations.
Quick Example
#!/bin/bash
# hello.sh
echo "Hello from script"
Commands to run in a terminal to try: chmod +x hello.sh then ./hello.sh. Check the exit status with echo "$?" after running.
Common Mistake
Forgetting to make the script executable or assuming running script name without a path will execute the file. Always use ./ for current directory or set PATH intentionally. Also avoid mixing sh-only constructs with bash-specific features unless you require bash.
Key Takeaway

Shebang and executable permission make script behavior consistent; test scripts by checking exit codes and edge cases.

screens.title: Variables in Bash: declaration and expansion
screens.narratorSegment: Variables store data that scripts use and modify. In Bash you create a variable by assigning a value with no spaces around the equals sign, for example NAME equals quote Alice quote. You reference a variable by prefixing its name with a dollar sign, like echo Hello comma dollar NAME. When combining variables with text, use braces to disambiguate, for example open curly brace NAME close curly brace underscore world to avoid the shell interpreting NAME underscore as a different token. A frequent issue is leaving variables unquoted in contexts where they may contain spaces or glob characters. Always quote variable expansions in tests and when passing values to commands to avoid word splitting and unexpected filename expansion. For numeric arithmetic, use double parentheses which perform integer math safely. Positional parameters are also variables: dollar one and dollar two hold the script arguments. Practice: assign a NAME with a space, then try echo both quoted and unquoted to observe differences. Remember also that variable names are case-sensitive and by convention uppercase for configuration-like values. What variable would you use to pass a directory path into your script?

keyIdea.title: Quote and brace
keyIdea.text: Assign with equals, expand with dollar, and protect values with quotes and braces to avoid splitting and globbing bugs.

content.html:
Declaration & Expansion
NAME="Alice"
echo "Hello, $NAME"
# Use braces when concatenating
echo "${NAME}_world"
Best practice: quote expansions like "${VAR}" when values may contain spaces or special characters.
Arithmetic
COUNT=0
COUNT=$((COUNT + 1))
if (( COUNT > 5 )); then
  echo "More than five"
fi
Use double parentheses for integer math. Do not use string operators for numeric tests.
Positional Parameters
# script.sh
echo "Script name: $0"
echo "First arg: $1"
echo "All args: $@"
echo "Arg count: $#"
Use "$@" to iterate over arguments without losing spacing, and use "$#" to check if enough arguments were provided.
Key Takeaway

Assign and expand carefully. Quote variable expansions and use braces to avoid ambiguity when concatenating text.

screens.title: Special variables: positional parameters and status codes
screens.narratorSegment: Special variables in Bash provide essential metadata to scripts. The script name is available as dollar zero, and positional parameters like dollar one and dollar two hold arguments passed to the script. Dollar at expands to all arguments preserving separation, and dollar hash returns the number of arguments. The exit status of the last command is dollar question mark, which is crucial for detecting success or failure: by convention zero means success and non-zero means an error. Dollar dollar gives the process ID of the current shell, which can be helpful when creating temporary files with predictable names. A concrete example: after running a critical command you can check if dollar question mark equals zero and proceed, or print an error and exit with a non-zero code. A common misconception is treating dollar at and dollar asterisk the same; dollar at preserves argument boundaries when quoted. Always quote "$@" when iterating over parameters. Use these variables to build robust scripts that validate inputs and respond to errors instead of silently continuing. Special variables: positional parameters and status codes means special variables let scripts read their arguments, count them, check success, and manage process-scoped data safely.. In practical terms, how $0, $1, $@, $#, $?, and $$ help scripts interact with their environment.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Metadata for scripts
keyIdea.text: Special variables let scripts read their arguments, count them, check success, and manage process-scoped data safely.

content.html:
Special Variables
  • $0 — script name
  • $1, $2, ... — positional arguments
  • $# — argument count
  • $@ — all arguments as separate words
  • $? — exit status of last command
  • $$ — PID of the current shell
Examples
# show args
for arg in "$@"; do
  echo "Arg: $arg"
done

# check last command
some_command
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Command failed"
  exit 1
fi
Prefer checking "$?" immediately after the command or use the conditional directly: if some_command; then ... fi.
Practical Tip

Use "$@" when forwarding arguments to other commands. Use $$ for temporary filenames but ensure cleanup to avoid collisions.

screens.title: Quoting and test operators
screens.narratorSegment: Tests in Bash come in two flavors: string and numeric, and using the wrong one or omitting quotes leads to bugs. String comparisons use double equals for equality and operators like dash z to check for empty strings. Numeric tests use dash eq, dash ne, dash gt and the like. For example, testing if a variable equals zero requires a numeric operator, not double equals in brackets. Another best practice is quoting variable expansions inside tests: [ "$VAR" == "value" ] or [ -z "${VAR}" ]. Quoting prevents word splitting and globbing if VAR contains spaces or wildcard characters. A useful contrast: double square brackets offer extra features such as pattern matching with =~ and are less brittle with certain expansions, but single square brackets are more portable in strictly POSIX contexts. Misusing == for numbers or failing to quote variables will produce unexpected results or syntax errors. Practice converting one test from string to numeric and observe the different behavior when VAR is empty or contains spaces. Final takeaway: pick the correct operator and always quote expansions inside tests to keep logic reliable.

keyIdea.title: Pick the right test
keyIdea.text: Use string operators for text, numeric operators for numbers, and always quote expansions to avoid splitting and globbing errors.

content.html:
String Tests
if [ -z "$NAME" ]; then
  echo "Name is empty"
fi

if [ "$USER" == "root" ]; then
  echo "Running as root"
fi
Quote variables inside brackets to avoid surprise when values contain spaces or are unset.
Numeric Tests
if [ "$COUNT" -gt 5 ]; then
  echo "Too many"
fi

# Or use arithmetic expression
if (( COUNT > 5 )); then
  echo "Too many"
fi
Do not use == for numeric comparison; use -eq, -ne, -gt, -lt or (( ... )).
Common Mistake

Using string operators for numeric tests or leaving variables unquoted leads to incorrect branch selection and subtle bugs.

screens.title: Using for and while loops
screens.narratorSegment: Loops let scripts repeat actions rather than copy and paste commands. The for loop is most commonly used to iterate over lists or globbed filenames. For example, for FILE in slash var slash log slash asterisk dot log semicolon do echo Processing dollar FILE done will iterate through matching files. When using globs, be mindful of the case where no matches are found; quoting can change behavior. Use for when you have a defined list or set of filenames. The while loop repeats as long as a condition holds; it is useful for counters or reading lines from a file. For example, initialize a counter and increment it inside a while loop until a limit is reached. A common pitfall is modifying the loop variable in a way that breaks iteration or failing to quote expansions when passing filenames to commands. Also avoid using for to parse whitespace-separated text when entries may contain spaces — instead use a while read loop to read lines safely. Practice both patterns: iterate over /etc/*. conf with a for loop, and read lines from a file using while read -r line to preserve backslashes and leading spaces. Which loop would you choose for processing filenames that may contain spaces?

keyIdea.title: Choose the right loop
keyIdea.text: Use for for simple lists and globs; use while read for line-oriented data or when entries may contain spaces.

content.html:
For loop example
for FILE in /var/log/*.log; do
  echo "Processing $FILE"
  # process "$FILE" safely here
done
If filenames may contain spaces, ensure commands you call quote the variable: "${FILE}".
While read example
while IFS= read -r LINE; do
  echo "Line: $LINE"
done < file.txt
Use IFS and -r to preserve leading/trailing spaces and backslashes when reading lines.
Check Your Understanding

When processing filenames with spaces, prefer a while read loop or ensure the for loop and commands quote expansions correctly.

screens.title: Input, output, and redirection
screens.narratorSegment: Input and output patterns allow scripts to communicate with users and files. Use echo to print messages and read to capture interactive input; for example, echo Enter your name followed by read NAME stores the response. Redirection operators control where streams go: greater-than overwrites a file, double greater-than appends, less-than feeds a file as standard input, and two greater-than number one redirects standard error. For example, command greater-than output dot txt redirects standard output, while command greater-than output dot txt two greater-than ampersand one will combine error and output. A best practice is to redirect output of commands you intend to save and capture non-zero exit codes to detect failures. When writing scripts that run unattended, avoid interactive read calls unless you explicitly check for terminal presence; instead accept arguments and validate them with positional parameters. A common mistake is accidentally overwriting important files with a single greater-than. Prefer appending when preserving logs or write to temporary files and rename atomically. Demonstrate these patterns and always test redirection on a safe target before using in production. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Full Script
#!/bin/bash

# Check if a directory path is provided as an argument
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 "
    exit 1
fi

TARGET_DIR="$1"

# Check if the provided path is a valid directory
if [ ! -d "$TARGET_DIR" ]; then
    echo "Error: '$TARGET_DIR' is not a valid directory."
    exit 2
fi

echo "Analyzing directory: $TARGET_DIR"

# Count files and subdirectories
NUM_FILES=$(find "$TARGET_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f | wc -l)
NUM_DIRS=$(find "$TARGET_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type d | wc -l)
# Subtract 1 from NUM_DIRS because 'find' counts the target directory itself
NUM_DIRS=$((NUM_DIRS - 1))

# Calculate disk usage
DISK_USAGE=$(du -sh "$TARGET_DIR" | awk '{print $1}')

echo "-------------------------------------"
echo "Number of files: $NUM_FILES"
echo "Number of subdirectories: $NUM_DIRS"
echo "Total disk usage: $DISK_USAGE"
echo "-------------------------------------"

exit 0

In this lesson you will learn why Bash scripting matters for system administration and how to get started safely. Bash is more than an interactive shell: it is a scripting language that lets you sequence commands, use variables, make decisions, loop over items, and redirect input and output. That combination is what makes repetitive maintenance, log processing, and simple orchestration reliable and repeatable. You will see how the shebang selects the interpreter, why making a script executable matters, and how comments and small tests make scripts maintainable. We will work through variable usage, including positional parameters and special variables such as the exit status, and explore conditionals, loops, and redirection patterns you will use every day. Along the way you will practice a hands-on script that analyzes a directory for counts and disk usage, and you will learn common pitfalls like failing to quote variables or mixing string and numeric operators. By the end, you will be able to write, run, and troubleshoot small Bash scripts that save time and reduce mistakes. Think about one repetitive task you do now — scripting it is the next step.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately. First, you will explain why Bash scripting is central to Linux administration: it lets you automate repetitive tasks, reduce human error, and capture knowledge in reusable scripts. As an example, think of a daily log rotation check that you can turn into a script and run automatically. Second, you will write basic Bash scripts: you will include a shebang so the OS invokes the intended interpreter, add comments for maintainability, set executable permissions, and run scripts from the shell. Practice creating a simple script that prints a startup message, then make it executable and run it. Third, you will declare and use variables: assign values, reference them with the dollar sign, and use braces to avoid ambiguity when concatenating strings. Fourth, you will understand key special variables such as positional parameters, the argument count, and the last command exit status. Each skill is framed with why it matters and a small mnemonic so you can recall correct practice under pressure.

In the second set of objectives you will learn to implement basic conditional logic with if, elif, and else, and to use test operators safely for strings, numbers, and files. You will practice quoting variables in tests to avoid word splitting and globbing errors. Next, you will use loops — the for loop to iterate over lists and files, and the while loop to repeat actions while a condition is true. A common scenario is processing log files or counting resources. You will also practice input and output: using echo to display messages, read to gather user input, and redirection operators to capture or append output to files. Finally, you will test scripts incrementally and check exit statuses to handle errors gracefully. Each objective includes a short why-it-matters note and a mnemonic to help you remember correct idioms under time pressure during exam tasks or real-world troubleshooting.

Bash, short for the Bourne Again SHell, is both an interactive command interpreter and a scripting language used across Linux systems. As an interpreter it runs commands you type; as a scripting language it executes statements saved in a file, so you can repeat tasks reliably. Automation is the reason we script: repetitive operations like backups, log rotation checks, or user provisioning are error-prone when done manually. A script captures the correct sequence and lets you run it unattended. For example, a short script that archives logs and rotates permissions will run the same way every time, eliminating small mistakes. A common misconception is that Bash is only for ad-hoc commands; in reality, small to medium automation tasks are an ideal fit. Another misconception is confusion between systemd timers and Bash scripts — they complement each other: timers schedule, scripts perform the work. When beginning, favor clear, well-commented scripts that test exit codes and report failures. Finally, remember portability: using the shebang and POSIX-compatible constructs helps scripts behave consistently across distributions. How might scripting one routine task today free time for higher-value work?

Script execution starts with the shebang line. The shebang is a special first line beginning with a hash and exclamation mark followed by the interpreter path, typically /bin/bash. It tells the kernel which program should interpret the script when you run it directly. Without the shebang, the system may default to another shell or require you to invoke the interpreter explicitly. After saving a script, you must set the executable bit using chmod +x so the kernel permits execution. Running a script from the current directory requires an explicit path like dot-slash script name to avoid running a same-named command from the PATH. A common workflow: create the file, add a concise shebang and comments, chmod it executable, and then run small tests. Check the exit status variable after critical operations to detect failures. A frequent mistake is forgetting chmod or assuming the shell will auto-detect the interpreter. Another issue is using a non-portable shebang path; when portability matters, use env in the shebang to locate bash. Practice: create a tiny script that prints a message, chmod it, and run it with different users to observe permission behavior. What step would you add to validate the script before production?

Variables store data that scripts use and modify. In Bash you create a variable by assigning a value with no spaces around the equals sign, for example NAME equals quote Alice quote. You reference a variable by prefixing its name with a dollar sign, like echo Hello comma dollar NAME. When combining variables with text, use braces to disambiguate, for example open curly brace NAME close curly brace underscore world to avoid the shell interpreting NAME underscore as a different token. A frequent issue is leaving variables unquoted in contexts where they may contain spaces or glob characters. Always quote variable expansions in tests and when passing values to commands to avoid word splitting and unexpected filename expansion. For numeric arithmetic, use double parentheses which perform integer math safely. Positional parameters are also variables: dollar one and dollar two hold the script arguments. Practice: assign a NAME with a space, then try echo both quoted and unquoted to observe differences. Remember also that variable names are case-sensitive and by convention uppercase for configuration-like values. What variable would you use to pass a directory path into your script?

Special variables in Bash provide essential metadata to scripts. The script name is available as dollar zero, and positional parameters like dollar one and dollar two hold arguments passed to the script. Dollar at expands to all arguments preserving separation, and dollar hash returns the number of arguments. The exit status of the last command is dollar question mark, which is crucial for detecting success or failure: by convention zero means success and non-zero means an error. Dollar dollar gives the process ID of the current shell, which can be helpful when creating temporary files with predictable names. A concrete example: after running a critical command you can check if dollar question mark equals zero and proceed, or print an error and exit with a non-zero code. Tests in Bash come in two flavors: string and numeric, and using the wrong one or omitting quotes leads to bugs. String comparisons use double equals for equality and operators like dash z to check for empty strings. Numeric tests use dash eq, dash ne, dash gt and the like. For example, testing if a variable equals zero requires a numeric operator, not double equals in brackets. Another best practice is quoting variable expansions inside tests: [ "$VAR" == "value" ] or [ -z "${VAR}" ]. Quoting prevents word splitting and globbing if VAR contains spaces or wildcard characters. Loops let scripts repeat actions rather than copy and paste commands. The for loop is most commonly used to iterate over lists or globbed filenames. For example, for FILE in slash var slash log slash asterisk dot log semicolon do echo Processing dollar FILE done will iterate through matching files. The while loop repeats as long as a condition holds; it is useful for counters or reading lines from a file.
